summary: Discusses three views of byte size for network connections: it should not be used at all, it is only for the NCP's convenience, or it is a user-level choice. The authors explain why the first view was dropped during the Host-Host protocol cleanup in RFC 107.

plainLanguage.summary: How should we cut bread: not at all, in whatever size is easiest for the baker, or the way the customer likes? This note weighs the three.

subtitle: Three views on whether byte size for network connections belongs to the NCP or to user processes.

tldr.problem: RFC 107 let the sending NCP choose a byte size for each connection, and it was unclear who should control that choice.
tldr.mechanism: The authors compare three views: no byte size at all, byte size as an NCP convenience, or byte size as a user-level choice. They argue for the third and discuss fixing byte sizes in third level protocols.
tldr.outcome: They conclude user processes must be able to specify byte size, and suggest setting the bit stream versus byte stream question aside until a major Host-Host Protocol overhaul.

facts.label: Byte sizes NCPs need not all support

today: The text does not record a formal status for RFC 176 (the metadata lists it as Unknown), and no later RFC is listed as replacing it. It comments on RFC 107.

sections.title: Three Views of Byte Size
sections.content:
Byte size for a connection is the byte size selected by the sending NCP, as explained in RFC 107. The RFC lists three views of it.

  • Byte size should not be used at all: connections are bit streams and messages carry bit counts (a byte size of 1). This view predates the "Glitch Cleaning" of RFC 107 and was dropped for efficiency in storage management and message concatenation.
  • Byte size is solely for the convenience of NCPs, a 2nd level issue. Third level user processes need not be able to specify it. The RFC says RFC 151 indicates this view.
  • Byte size is a user-level prerogative, chosen explicitly or implicitly through I/O mode. An NCP may use a default if the user gives none.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three ideas: cut the bread into crumbs, let the baker pick the slice size, or let the eater pick.

sections.title: Why the User-Level View Is Correct
sections.content:
The authors say the third view is the correct reading of RFC 107, which states on page 2 that choosing byte size is a 3rd level protocol issue. Protocols such as TELNET and ICP require a specific byte size, so their processes must be able to specify and impose it on the NCP. NCP implementors should take note.

Restricting the choice to NCPs also risks a byte size mismatch at the user-NCP interface, not just between the communicating NCPs.
sections.plainLanguage: Whoever uses the data knows best how it should be cut, so they should get to say.

sections.title: Fixed Byte Sizes in Third Level Protocols
sections.content:
Should a 3rd level protocol fix one byte size? Two arguments in favour: RFC 107 does not require NCPs to handle all byte sizes 1 through 255, and a fixed size of 8 bits or multiples of 8 is acceptable to all hosts, including terminal IMPs. Also, agreeing beforehand can reduce program space and possibly run time.

For TELNET (8-bit ASCII characters) and ICP (32-bit socket numbers) the choice is simple. For data transfer protocols it is harder: a mismatched byte size reduces efficiency and needs filler fields for blocks that are not a multiple of the size. Since byte size is fixed for the life of a connection, varying data structure remains a problem.

The authors still judge that fixing byte size in 3rd level protocols is a good idea for now.
sections.plainLanguage: Using one standard slice size means everyone can handle it, but it wastes some bread when your food does not fit that size.

sections.title: Reopening the Byte Stream Question
sections.content:
The discussion exposes weaknesses in the efficiency arguments for byte streams. Moving from bit stream to byte stream may have lost generality, and it is unclear how much overall efficiency was gained. The combined efficiency of NCP and user processes matters, not NCP efficiency alone.

The authors' opinion is that the bit stream versus byte stream issue should be set aside until serious consideration can be given to a major Host-Host Protocol overhaul.
sections.plainLanguage: Maybe cutting bread at all was not the best idea, but let us decide that when we rebuild the bakery.

references.text: RFC 107, the output of the Host-Host Protocol Glitch Cleaning Committee.
RFC 151, by Shoshani, cited for the view that byte size is an NCP issue.
